passages: Many people in Taiwan start their day at a breakfast shop. These small shops open very early, some as early as five in the morning, and they sell everything from egg pancakes to sandwiches and soy milk. For busy students and office workers, breakfast shops are convenient and cheap. However, some doctors worry that many popular breakfast foods contain too much oil and sugar. They suggest choosing items with more vegetables and protein, and drinking unsweetened soy milk or water instead of sweet milk tea. A healthy breakfast, they say, gives people more energy and helps them focus better at school or work.

Last month, our city library started a new program called "Read with a Volunteer." Every Saturday afternoon, children can come to the library and read stories with retired teachers, nurses, and other volunteers. The program was created because many parents work on weekends and have little time to read with their children. So far, the response has been very positive. More than two hundred children have joined, and several volunteers say that the program has made them feel useful and connected to their community. The library hopes to start a similar program for elderly people who have trouble reading small print.

passages: More and more young people in Taiwan are choosing to ride bicycles to work or school. Cycling is good for the environment because it does not produce air pollution, and it is also a great way to exercise. Many cities now have bike-sharing systems, so people can rent a bike for a short time at a low price. However, cycling on busy streets can be dangerous. Riders should always wear a helmet, follow traffic rules, and use lights at night. If the government builds more bike lanes, even more people may feel safe enough to leave their cars and scooters at home.

Sleep is just as important as food and exercise, but many students do not get enough of it. Some stay up late to study for exams, while others spend hours watching videos or playing games on their phones. Without enough sleep, it is harder to remember new information, and people are more likely to catch colds. Experts suggest that teenagers sleep eight to ten hours a night. They also recommend putting phones away at least thirty minutes before bed and going to sleep at the same time every day. Small changes like these can make a big difference.

passages: Convenience stores are everywhere in Taiwan, and they offer much more than snacks and drinks. People can pay their bills, pick up packages, print documents, and buy train tickets there. Many stores are open twenty-four hours a day, which makes them very useful for night workers and students. Some stores also have seats where customers can eat a simple meal or charge their phones. Visitors from other countries are often surprised by how many services one small shop can provide. For many people in Taiwan, the convenience store has become a part of daily life.

Nurses play an important role in hospitals, but their work is often harder than people imagine. A nurse may take care of eight or more patients in one shift. Besides giving medicine and checking vital signs, nurses also talk with worried family members, teach patients how to take care of themselves at home, and write detailed records. Because hospitals are open day and night, many nurses work long hours or night shifts. In recent years, some hospitals have tried to hire more nurses and use new technology to reduce paperwork, so that nurses can spend more time with their patients.
